corrected_value.authors: Mazor M, Friston KJ, Fleming SM.
corrected_value.title: Distinct neural contributions to metacognition for detecting, but not discriminating visual stimuli.

decisions.quote: In a previous study we identified distinct neural contributions to confidence in perceptual detection that were not observed in a performance-matched discrimination task. In this pre-registered follow-up study, we set out to replicate this finding and to further characterize the computational origins of a quadratic modulation of confidence. In what follows, we summarize our findings, discuss how our previous conclusions should be revised in light of this new data and unpack what this may mean for our understanding of a quadratic effect of decision confidence in association cortex.3.1. A quadratic modulation of confidence is not distinct to perceptual detectionAs in Mazor et al. [6], here too we observed a widespread quadratic modulation of subjective confidence in prefrontal and parietal association cortex.

decisions.reason: The abstract contains a year typo ('Mazor et al. 2021') when describing the original fMRI study, which caused the shipped coding to misidentify the target as Reference 15 (Mazor, Moran & Fleming, 2021, 10.1093/nc/niab025, cited only once in line 16 as background on behavioural metacognitive sensitivity). The body text, ROI definitions, and pre-registered objectives explicitly identify Reference 6 (Mazor, Friston & Fleming, 2020, eLife, 10.7554/eLife.53900) as the original fMRI study being replicated.

decisions.quote: Here, in a pre-registered follow-up experiment, we sought to replicate our original findings and identify the origins of putative detection-specific confidence signals by introducing a novel asymmetric-discrimination condition. The new condition required discriminating two alternatives but was engineered such that the distribution of perceptual evidence was asymmetric, just as in yes/no detection. We successfully replicated the quadratic modulation of subjective confidence in prefrontal, parietal and temporal cortices. However, in contrast with our original report, this quadratic effect was similar in detection and discrimination responses, but stronger in the novel asymmetric-discrimination condition. We interpret our findings as weighing against the detection-specificity of confidence signatures and speculate about possible alternative origins of a quadratic modulation of decision confidence.
decisions.location: abstract (line 13); see also Introduction (line 15), Results Section 2.2.1 & 2.2.3 (lines 16-17), and Discussion Section 3.1, 3.2 & 3.5 (line 19)
decisions.reason: For the resolved original study (Mazor, Friston & Fleming, 2020 [6]), the authors explicitly report replicating the main positive quadratic effect of subjective confidence across prefrontal, parietal, and temporal cortices (as well as linear confidence effects in pre-specified ROIs), but fail to replicate the interaction with task (detection vs. discrimination specificity) and the rTPJ detection response asymmetry, explicitly contrasting these null interactions with the original report ('However, in contrast with our original report...'). Per the codebook, replicating the main effect while failing to replicate the interactions is coded as 'mixed'.
